intro.text: Six pages for the first church at Jerusalem and the witnesses who went out from it: James and Jude, two of the Lord's brothers; Stephen and Philip, two of the Seven; Barnabas, and his relative John Mark.

None of the six is in the lists of the Twelve. Luke calls Barnabas an apostle with Paul (Acts 14:14); Paul names “James the Lord's brother” when he speaks of the apostles he saw (Galatians 1:19), and what that makes James is a question on his page.
Same names, different men: this James is not the son of Zebedee, whom Herod killed (Acts 12:2), and this Philip is not the apostle. Early writers sometimes confused them, and the pages say where.

Scripture records the death of only one of them, Stephen (Acts 7:59-60). What is told of the others' later lives comes from Josephus, from church writers of the 2nd to 5th centuries, and from later legends; every such line names who said it and when.

apostles.name: James, the Lord's brother
otherNames: James the Just (a name from Hegesippus, not from Scripture)
apostles.title: The Lord's brother (Galatians 1:19)
apostles.tagline: Named first of Jesus' brothers; later one of the “pillars” of the church in Jerusalem.

home.text: He is named among the family the people of Jesus' “own country” knew (Mark 6:1-3). Acts and Galatians later find him in Jerusalem every time (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:18-19; 2:9).

family.text: At Nazareth the people name Jesus' brothers: “James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon”, with sisters who are not named.
Mary the mother of Jesus is named with the brothers in the upper room after the ascension.
The letter of Jude opens “Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James”; it does not say which James.

Scripture does not say how James and the other brothers were related to Mary and Joseph; the three answers given are set out below. Our person data lists Joseph and Mary as his parents, which is one of those answers.

identifications.text: After Acts 1:13 two men called James act in Acts: James the brother of John, killed by Herod (Acts 12:2), and the James to whom Peter sends word in the same chapter and who later speaks at the council (Acts 12:17; 15:13). James son of Alphaeus is named only in the list of Acts 1:13.

That this James of Acts is the one Paul calls “the Lord's brother” comes from setting Acts beside Galatians, where James, Cephas and John are the “pillars” (Galatians 1:19; 2:9). Lightfoot (1890) and McGiffert (1890) both read them as one man.

“The Just” is not a name Scripture gives him. Hegesippus (about AD 170), quoted by Eusebius, says he “has been called the Just by all from the time of our Saviour to the present day; for there were many that bore the name of James.”
Paul writes that the risen Lord “was seen of James” (1 Corinthians 15:7) but does not say which James.
Eusebius takes that James to be the Lord's brother: “he appeared unto James, who was one of the so-called brethren of the Saviour”.

A story first found in the lost Gospel according to the Hebrews, which Jerome (392) quotes: James had sworn not to eat bread until he saw the Lord risen, and the risen Lord took bread, blessed it and gave it to him, saying “my brother eat thy bread, for the son of man is risen from among those that sleep.”

Hegesippus (about AD 170) also draws James as a lifelong ascetic: “he drank no wine nor strong drink, nor did he eat flesh”, wore linen, was “permitted to enter into the holy place”, and prayed so much that “his knees became hard like those of a camel”. McGiffert (1890) quotes Schaff's verdict that this is “an overdrawn picture”.

moments.label: Named first of his brothers at Nazareth
His mother and brothers come asking for Jesus (the brothers are not named)
With his mother and brothers at Capernaum (the brothers are not named)
“Neither did his brethren believe in him” (the brothers are not named)
The risen Lord “was seen of James” (which James is not said)

acts.text: After the ascension the Lord's brothers pray with the apostles, the women and Mary the mother of Jesus.
“After three years” Paul spent fifteen days with Peter in Jerusalem and saw none of the other apostles “save James the Lord's brother”.
Freed from prison, Peter tells the believers at the house of John Mark's mother: “Go shew these things unto James, and to the brethren.”

At the Jerusalem council, after Peter, Barnabas and Paul have spoken, James answers: he quotes the prophets on the Gentiles, says “my sentence is, that we trouble not them”, and proposes the letter on idols, fornication, things strangled and blood. The apostles, elders and whole church agree.
Paul says that James, Cephas and John, “who seemed to be pillars”, gave him and Barnabas “the right hands of fellowship”, asking only that they remember the poor.
At Antioch Peter ate with Gentiles until “certain came from James”; then he withdrew, and the other Jews and even Barnabas went with him.
On Paul's last visit to Jerusalem he goes in to James with all the elders present; they glorify God for his report and ask him to join four men in a vow, so all may know he keeps the law.
Paul speaks of “the brethren of the Lord” having the right “to lead about a sister, a wife”, as the other apostles and Cephas did; he names none of them.
The letter of James opens “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” and does not say which James wrote it; that question belongs to the Letters page.
The last verse that shows James alive is Acts 21:18. Scripture does not record his death.

places.name: Nazareth
places.note: Jesus' “own country” (Mark 6:1), where the people named his brothers; Mark names Nazareth as the town Jesus came from (Mark 1:9).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where Scripture always finds him after the resurrection.

places.name: Antioch
places.note: Men “came from James” to Antioch in Syria (he is not said to have gone there).

places.name: Jerusalem: the temple (his death, in Hegesippus's account)
places.note: Hegesippus (about 170): thrown from the pinnacle of the temple and buried “on the spot, by the temple”.

claim.text: Paul stayed with Peter and saw James on the same visit; Peter sends news of his escape to James; both speak at the council; both are “pillars”.
The third of the “pillars” with James and Cephas.
Saw him in Jerusalem after his conversion, received “the right hands of fellowship”, and reported to him on his last visit.
Spoke before James at the council and received the right hand of fellowship with Paul.
Chosen to carry the council's letter to Antioch after James's proposal.
Named with him among the brothers.
Named with the brothers in the upper room.

Hegesippus (about 170) says that after James's death Symeon, son of the Lord's uncle Clopas, was chosen the next bishop of Jerusalem, “because he was a cousin of the Lord”. Eusebius repeats it, “as they say”.

scripture.text: Scripture does not record how or when James died. The last we see of him is the meeting with Paul and the elders in Jerusalem (Acts 21:18-25).

tradition.text: When Festus was dead and Albinus “but upon the road”, the high priest Ananus “assembled the sanhedrim of judges, and brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others”, and “delivered them to be stoned”. Some citizens protested; Agrippa took the high priesthood from Ananus after three months.
tradition.who: Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1 (trans. Whiston, 1737)
tradition.when: written about AD 93; the events about 62

tradition.text: James was set on the pinnacle of the temple at Passover and asked to turn the people from Jesus; he answered that Jesus “sitteth in heaven at the right hand of the great Power”. He was thrown down, stoned, prayed “forgive them, for they know not what they do”, and was struck dead with a fuller's club. “And immediately Vespasian besieged them.”
tradition.who: Hegesippus, Memoirs book 5, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 2.23.4-18

tradition.text: McGiffert (1890) points to “the legendary character of Hegesippus' account” in its details, such as the scribes asking James to calm the crowd, and quotes Schaff on his ascetic portrait of James: “an overdrawn picture from the middle of the second century”. He still accepts that James was stoned.
tradition.who: A. C. McGiffert, notes 493, 500 and 512 to Eusebius 2.23, quoting Philip Schaff

tradition.text: Clement of Alexandria wrote that James “was thrown from the pinnacle of the temple and was beaten to death with a club by a fuller”.
tradition.who: Clement of Alexandria, Hypotyposes book 7, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 2.1.4

tradition.text: Origen, and Eusebius after him, say that Josephus traced Jerusalem's sufferings to the death of James; in Eusebius's words they came “to avenge James the Just”. McGiffert notes that the sentence is not in the surviving manuscripts of Josephus; it is not in the Whiston text the project holds either.
tradition.who: Origen, Against Celsus 1.47 and 2.13; Eusebius, Church History 2.23.20
tradition.when: Origen about 245 or later; Eusebius about 325

tradition.text: Jerome says James “ruled the church of Jerusalem thirty years, that is until the seventh year of Nero, and was buried near the temple”, and that his tombstone was known until the siege of Titus and the end of Hadrian's reign.
tradition.who: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 2

tradition.text: Eusebius says the “chair of James” at Jerusalem “has been preserved until now”.
tradition.who: Eusebius, Church History 7.19

writings.title: The letter of James (which James wrote it is a question on the Letters page)

questions.question: Who were “the brethren of the Lord”? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage
views.holders: First found in the apocryphal Protevangelium of James (its stories go back to the 2nd century), where Joseph says “I have children”; Origen (about AD 245 or later), who reports that “some say” it, “basing it on a tradition in the Gospel according to Peter, as it is entitled, or ‘The Book of James’”; Eusebius (about 325), for whom James “was known as a son of Joseph”; some in Jerome's day (“as some think”); J. B. Lightfoot (1865, 10th ed. 1890), “the strongest advocate” of it in McGiffert's words; still the established view of the Greek Church, McGiffert (1890) notes

argument.text: Lightfoot's chief argument: on the cross Jesus gave his mother to “the disciple … whom he loved”, and “from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home” (John 19:26-27), which he finds hard to believe if she had sons of her own. McGiffert grants that this view “has the oldest tradition in its favor”, though none of the traditions, he adds, is old enough “to be of great weight”.

views.label: Younger sons of Joseph and Mary
views.holders: Tertullian (early 3rd century), whose argument, Lightfoot judges, “seems to imply” it; Helvidius (about 380), against whom Jerome wrote; A. C. McGiffert (1890), who names Andrews, Schaff and Weiss with him and notes that the view is “widely accepted in the Protestant Church”; H. E. Jacobs (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: The plain sense of “brother” and “sisters” beside “his mother” (Mark 6:3); Mary's “firstborn son” (Luke 2:7); and the brothers' unbelief (John 7:5), which, McGiffert argues, keeps them out of the Twelve.

views.label: Cousins: the sons of Mary the wife of Clopas
views.holders: Jerome, Against Helvidius (about AD 383); since then the established view of the Latin Church, McGiffert (1890) notes; W. H. Mill (1843), as reported by Lightfoot and McGiffert

argument.text: Jerome argues that Paul counts “James the Lord's brother” among the apostles, that only two apostles were called James, and so the Lord's “brethren” were kinsmen, sons of the Mary who stood at the cross (John 19:25).

questions.question: Does Paul count James among the apostles in Galatians 1:19? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: Yes: an apostle, but not one of the Twelve
views.holders: J. B. Lightfoot (1890); Eusebius (about 325), who says many besides the Twelve “were called apostles”

argument.text: Lightfoot reads “other of the apostles saw I none, save James” as naming James an apostle; the same James is not in the lists of the Twelve, and Acts 1:13-14 names the brothers apart from the apostles.

views.label: Yes, because he was one of the Twelve: James son of Alphaeus
views.holders: Jerome, Against Helvidius 15 (about AD 383); Clement of Alexandria (about 200), as McGiffert reads him

argument.text: If Paul calls him an apostle, and only two of the Twelve were named James, the Lord's brother must be the son of Alphaeus.

questions.question: When did James die? (In the order of the sources.)

views.label: About AD 62, by stoning, under the high priest Ananus
views.holders: Josephus's account as McGiffert (1890: “61 or 62”) and Kerr (ISBE, 1915: “about 62 or 63”) read it; Jerome (392) has “the seventh year of Nero”

argument.text: Josephus dates the trial between the death of Festus and the arrival of Albinus; McGiffert holds that this exact setting fixes the date.

views.label: Condemned then, but he “did not die till long afterwards”
views.holders: William Whiston, in a note to his translation (1737)

argument.text: Whiston argues that the Sanhedrin could not put a man to death without the Roman governor's approval, which Ananus never had.

views.label: Just before Vespasian's war (from AD 67)
views.holders: Hegesippus (about 170), who ends his account “And immediately Vespasian besieged them”; E. C. Richardson (1892), who gives “69 (Hegesippus)” beside “62 or 63 (according to Josephus and Jerome)”; McGiffert (1890) reports this reading but thinks “immediately” too loose to set a date

argument.text: Hegesippus links the death directly to the siege that followed, without giving a year.

notSaid: Scripture never calls him “the Just” or “bishop”; both titles come from the 2nd century and later.
Scripture does not say how he was related to Joseph and Mary, when he came to believe (only that the risen Lord “was seen of James”, if that is the same James), or whether he married.
Scripture does not say whether he wrote the letter that bears the name James.
Scripture does not record his death.

apostles.name: Jude, the Lord's brother
apostles.title: One of the Lord's brothers (Mark 6:3)
apostles.tagline: A name in the family list at Nazareth; Hegesippus tells of his grandsons brought before an emperor.

home.text: He is named among the family the people of Jesus' “own country” knew (Mark 6:1-3).

family.text: He is one of the four brothers the people at Nazareth name: “James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon”.
Mark spells the name “Juda”, Matthew “Judas”; the Greek is the same name, which the letter of Jude also uses.
Paul says “the brethren of the Lord” had the right “to lead about a sister, a wife”, as the other apostles did; he does not say which brothers.
Hegesippus (about AD 170) knew of grandsons of “Jude, who is said to have been the Lord's brother according to the flesh”.

identifications.text: This page is about the brother named at Nazareth (Mark 6:3). Two other men called Judas appear among the first disciples: Judas Iscariot, and the apostle “Judas the brother of James” (Luke 6:16), where “the brother” is a word the KJV supplies.

The letter of Jude opens “Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James”. It does not call its writer the Lord's brother, and it speaks of “the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ” as others (verse 17). Who wrote it is a question for the Letters page.
Origen (about AD 245 or later) reads the letter's opening as the words of this Jude, the brother of James and of the Lord.

His mother and brothers come asking for Jesus (the brothers are not named)
With his mother and brothers at Capernaum (the brothers are not named)
“Neither did his brethren believe in him” (the brothers are not named)

acts.text: After the ascension the Lord's brothers pray with the apostles, the women and Mary the mother of Jesus.
Paul names “the brethren of the Lord” with the other apostles and Cephas as having the right “to lead about a sister, a wife”.
Scripture names this Jude only in the two Nazareth lists (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55). Acts 1:14 and 1 Corinthians 9:5 speak of the brothers as a group.

places.note: Jesus' “own country” (Mark 6:1), where the people named his brothers; Mark names Nazareth as the town Jesus came from (Mark 1:9).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: With the other brothers in the upper room after the ascension.

Named with the brothers in the upper room.

Named with him among the brothers.

scripture.text: Scripture names Jude only in the Nazareth lists; after that the brothers appear only as a group (Acts 1:14). It records nothing of his death.

tradition.text: “Of the family of the Lord there were still living the grandchildren of Jude, who is said to have been the Lord's brother according to the flesh.” Accused of being of David's line, they were brought before the emperor Domitian; they owned only “a piece of land which contained only thirty-nine acres”, and supported themselves by their own labour.
tradition.who: Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.19-20

tradition.text: Eusebius adds, in his own words, that they showed their work-hardened hands, said Christ's kingdom was “not a temporal nor an earthly kingdom, but a heavenly and angelic one”, and were let go. McGiffert notes that the quotation from Hegesippus ends before this part.
tradition.who: Eusebius, Church History 3.20.5-7

tradition.text: “They came, therefore, and took the lead of every church as witnesses and as relatives of the Lord”, and lived until the reign of Trajan.
tradition.who: Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.32.5-6

tradition.text: Writers who took this Jude to be the apostle Thaddaeus gave him that apostle's story. The Golden Legend calls the apostle Judas “brother to James the Less” and has him and Simon cut down in Persia.
tradition.who: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend (Caxton's English, ed. Ellis 1900)

writings.title: The letter of Jude (who wrote it is a question on the Letters page)

questions.question: Is Jude the Lord's brother the same man as the apostle “Judas of James” (Thaddaeus)? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: Two different men
views.holders: A. C. McGiffert (1890); J. B. Lightfoot (1890), who notes that the writer of Jude “seems to disclaim for himself the title of an Apostle”

argument.text: The brothers did not believe in Jesus after the Twelve were chosen (John 7:5), and Acts 1:13-14 names the apostles and then, separately, “his brethren”. Luke's “Judas of James” is, McGiffert argues, the son of a James, not his brother.

views.label: The same man
views.holders: M. G. Easton (1897, under “Jude”), who lists Matthew 13:55 among the apostle's verses; the Golden Legend (about 1260); it follows from the cousin view, which counts the Lord's brothers among the Twelve, as H. E. Jacobs (ISBE, 1915) describes that view in full

argument.text: Read with the KJV as “Judas the brother of James” (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13), the apostle matches the Jude who calls himself “brother of James” (Jude 1) and the Judas named among the Lord's brothers (Matthew 13:55).

views.holders: First found in the apocryphal Protevangelium of James (its stories go back to the 2nd century), where Joseph says “I have children”; Origen (about AD 245 or later), who reports that “some say” it, “basing it on a tradition in the Gospel according to Peter, as it is entitled, or ‘The Book of James’”; Eusebius (about 325), for whom James “was known as a son of Joseph”; some in Jerome's day (“as some think”); J. McGiffert grants that this view “has the oldest tradition in its favor”, though none of the traditions, he adds, is old enough “to be of great weight”.

views.label: Younger sons of Joseph and Mary
views.holders: Tertullian (early 3rd century), whose argument, Lightfoot judges, “seems to imply” it; Helvidius (about 380), against whom Jerome wrote; A. C. McGiffert (1890), who names Andrews, Schaff and Weiss with him and notes that the view is “widely accepted in the Protestant Church”; H. E. Jacobs (ISBE, 1915)

views.label: Cousins: the sons of Mary the wife of Clopas
views.holders: Jerome, Against Helvidius (about AD 383); since then the established view of the Latin Church, McGiffert (1890) notes; W. H. Mill (1843), as reported by Lightfoot and McGiffert

argument.text: Jerome argues that Paul counts “James the Lord's brother” among the apostles, that only two apostles were called James, and so the Lord's “brethren” were kinsmen, sons of the Mary who stood at the cross (John 19:25).

notSaid: Scripture records nothing Jude said or did as a person; he is a name in the Nazareth list and one of “his brethren”.
Scripture does not say how he was related to Joseph and Mary (see the question below), whether he travelled, or how he died.
Scripture does not say that he wrote the letter of Jude.

apostles.name: Stephen
apostles.title: One of the Seven (Acts 6:5)
apostles.tagline: “Full of faith and of the Holy Ghost”; stoned outside Jerusalem, praying for those who stoned him.

family.text: Scripture names no family, home town or trade for Stephen.

identifications.text: He is first named when the Seven are chosen (Acts 6:5) and appears only in Acts; the person page and this page are the same man.
Eusebius (about AD 325) notes that he was the first “to receive the crown, corresponding to his name”: Stephanos is Greek for a crown.
Whether he was a Greek-speaking Jew is not said. Souvay (1912) writes that his Greek name “suggests he was a Hellenist”; Press (ISBE, 1915) that his name and place in the church “seem to imply” it.
A tradition of the 5th century, reported by Souvay, makes Stephanos the Greek for an Aramaic name, Kelil (“crown”), which “may be” his original name and was cut on a slab found in his tomb.

Later lists make him one of the Seventy (Luke 10:1): Epiphanius in the 4th century, and the list “On the Seventy Apostles” printed among the doubtful works of Hippolytus, which calls him “the first martyr”. Souvay doubts whether Epiphanius is “deserving of any credence”.

quote.text: they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch

claim.text: When the Grecians complained that their widows were neglected in the daily ministration, the Twelve asked the disciples to choose seven men “of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom”; the apostles prayed and laid their hands on them.

acts.text: “Full of faith and power”, he “did great wonders and miracles among the people”.
Men of the synagogue of the Libertines, and of Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and those of Cilicia and Asia disputed with him and “were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake”.

They brought him before the council with false witnesses, who said he spoke against “this holy place, and the law”, and that Jesus would destroy the place and change the customs of Moses. The council “saw his face as it had been the face of an angel”.

Asked by the high priest “Are these things so?”, he told Israel's story from Abraham through Joseph and Moses, “whom they refused”, to the tabernacle and Solomon's house; said “the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands”; and charged his hearers: “as your fathers did, so do ye”, calling them “the betrayers and murderers” of “the Just One”, who had received the law “and have not kept it”.
“Full of the Holy Ghost”, he looked up and said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God.”
They cast him out of the city and stoned him; the witnesses laid their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul, who “was consenting unto his death”.
A great persecution followed; all but the apostles were scattered through Judaea and Samaria, and some went as far as Phenice, Cyprus and Antioch, preaching the word.
Years later Paul told the crowd in Jerusalem: “when the blood of thy martyr Stephen was shed, I also was standing by”.

Stephen gives “threescore and fifteen souls” for Jacob's family going down to Egypt (Acts 7:14); Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 give seventy. The Greek Septuagint, in the site's text, reads seventy-five in both places. He also says the patriarchs were laid at Sychem in a tomb “that Abraham bought” (Acts 7:16); Genesis has Abraham buying the cave of Machpelah and Jacob buying the ground at Shechem.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Chosen, tried before the council, and stoned “out of the city”.

places.name: Cyrene
places.note: Home of one of the synagogue groups that disputed with him.

places.name: Alexandria
places.note: Home of one of the synagogue groups that disputed with him.

places.name: Cilicia
places.note: Home of one of the synagogue groups that disputed with him (Saul was of Tarsus in Cilicia, Acts 22:3).

places.name: Phoenicia
places.note: Reached by those scattered “upon the persecution that arose about Stephen”.

places.name: Cyprus
places.note: Reached by those scattered after his death.

places.name: Antioch
places.note: Reached by those scattered after his death; there some began to preach to the Grecians.

places.name: Caphar Gamala (his tomb, in tradition)
places.note: Where, Souvay reports, the priest Lucian said in 415 the body had been revealed to him; not in the atlas.

claim.text: Chosen with him as one of the Seven.
One of the Seven.
One of the Seven.
One of the Seven.
One of the Seven.
One of the Seven.
Kept the clothes of those who stoned him and consented to his death; later called him “thy martyr Stephen”.

scripture.text: Stoned outside the city, he prayed “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit”, knelt and cried “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep.”
“Devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him.”
His is the first killing of a disciple for his witness that Acts records, and the only death of anyone on these six pages that Scripture tells.

tradition.text: Irenaeus calls him the one “who, of all men, was the first to follow the footsteps of the martyrdom of the Lord, being the first that was slain for confessing Christ”.
tradition.who: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.12.10

tradition.text: In 415 a priest named Lucian said he had learned by revelation that the body lay at Caphar Gamala, north of Jerusalem; the relics were moved to the church on Mount Sion.
tradition.who: Lucian's account, as reported by Souvay (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1912)

tradition.text: In 460 the relics went to a basilica built by the empress Eudocia outside the Damascus Gate, where tradition placed the stoning; the idea that he died east of the city, by the gate now called St. Stephen's, Souvay says, “is unheard of until the twelfth century”.
tradition.who: Reported by Souvay (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1912)
tradition.when: AD 460; the eastern site from the 12th century

questions.question: Were the Seven the first “deacons”? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Yes: the first deacons
views.holders: Irenaeus (about AD 180), the first known to say so; Cyprian; “almost all scholars” in McGiffert's day, Lightfoot among them; Easton (1897); Souvay (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1912)

argument.text: Irenaeus calls Stephen the one “who was chosen the first deacon by the apostles”. Acts uses the related words for their “daily ministration” and to “serve tables”.

views.label: No: an office for this one task
views.holders: John Chrysostom (Homily 14 on Acts, about AD 400); in modern times Vitringa and Stanley, as reported by McGiffert

argument.text: Chrysostom asks whether theirs was the rank of deacons, and answers that “neither Deacons nor Presbyters is their designation: but it was for this particular purpose that they were ordained.”

views.label: No: the first of the Jerusalem “elders”
views.holders: Böhmer, Ritschl, Lange and Lechler, as reported by McGiffert; A. C. McGiffert (1890)

argument.text: Luke never calls the Seven deacons; the apostles' own work is called a “ministry” in the same passage; and when the elders first appear they receive the relief sent from Antioch, the kind of task the Seven were chosen for.

questions.question: When was Stephen killed? (Acts gives no year; scholars' dates.)

views.label: About AD 35
views.holders: A. T. Robertson (ISBE, 1915), who thinks 35 “more probable than 32 or 33”

argument.text: Robertson reasons from Saul, still “a young man” (Acts 7:58), and from Pilate, who was not deposed until AD 36 and was uneasy for a couple of years before, so less likely to stop the Jewish leaders acting outside the law. He grants that “nothing decisive is here obtained”.

views.label: About AD 36 or 37
views.holders: S. D. Press (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: Press dates it “c 36 or 37 AD” (that is, about 36 or 37) without setting out his reasons.

questions.question: Why does Stephen count “threescore and fifteen souls” where Genesis has seventy? (Order of the sources.)

views.label: He followed the Greek Septuagint
views.holders: Matthew Henry (on Acts 7), who compares Luke 3:36, where Cainan is “not in the Hebrew text, but in the Septuagint”

argument.text: Henry: “the Septuagint there makes them seventy-five, and Stephen or Luke follows that version”. The site's Septuagint reads seventy-five at Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5.

views.label: The two numbers count different people
views.holders: unnamed writers reported by Matthew Henry

argument.text: They leave out Joseph and his sons, who were already in Egypt, and add other members of the household, so the count comes to seventy-five.

notSaid: Scripture does not say where Stephen came from, how he came to believe, or whether he was a Greek-speaking Jew.
Acts does not call the Seven “deacons”; it says they were chosen to serve at the daily ministration.
Acts does not say whether the council passed sentence before the stoning, or where he was buried.

apostles.name: Philip the evangelist
apostles.title: “Philip the evangelist, which was one of the seven” (Acts 21:8)
apostles.tagline: Preached in Samaria, baptized an Ethiopian official on the Gaza road, and settled at Caesarea.

home.text: When Paul passed through, years after Acts 8, Philip had a house at Caesarea, where Paul's company stayed “many days”.

family.text: “The same man had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy.”
Scripture names no wife, parents or home town, and does not give the daughters' names.

identifications.text: This is not Philip the apostle, one of the Twelve (Matthew 10:3; John 1:43). Luke keeps them apart: the Seven were chosen so that the Twelve could keep to prayer and the word (Acts 6:2-5), and Acts 21:8 calls this man “one of the seven”.

The Philip who preached in Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian (Acts 8) is taken to be this Philip: all but the apostles had been scattered (Acts 8:1), the apostles at Jerusalem sent Peter and John to his converts (8:14), and Acts leaves him at Caesarea (8:40), where Philip the evangelist lives in Acts 21:8.

Early writers confused the two Philips. Polycrates (about AD 190) speaks of “Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who sleeps in Hierapolis” with his daughters; Eusebius (about 325) quotes him and then quotes Acts 21:8-9 about the evangelist's daughters as if of the same man.

McGiffert (1890) judges that “Philip the apostle and Philip the evangelist are here confounded”, and notes that Eusebius treats them as one man. Hunter (ISBE, 1915) also writes that in the Hierapolis tradition “in all probability the evangelist is confounded with the apostle”.

quote.text: they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip

claim.text: Chosen with Stephen and five others to serve at the daily ministration, men “of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom”; the apostles prayed and laid their hands on them.

quote.text: Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them.

claim.text: Scattered from Jerusalem by the persecution after Stephen's death, he became a preacher in Samaria.

acts.text: In Samaria the people heard him and saw the miracles: unclean spirits came out, the palsied and lame were healed, “and there was great joy in that city”.
Men and women believed and were baptized; Simon, who had used sorcery there, also believed, was baptized and “continued with Philip”.
The apostles at Jerusalem sent Peter and John, who prayed for the Samaritans to receive the Holy Ghost; Simon then offered them money.

An angel sent him toward the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza. There he met an Ethiopian eunuch, treasurer of Candace queen of the Ethiopians, reading Isaiah in his chariot; Philip “began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus”.
At a water the eunuch asked, “what doth hinder me to be baptized?” Philip baptized him; the Spirit “caught away Philip”, and the eunuch went on his way rejoicing.

Acts 8:37 (Philip's “If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest” and the eunuch's confession) is in the Greek text the KJV translated; Tischendorf's Greek and the Revised Version (1881) leave it out.
He was “found at Azotus”, and preached in all the cities until he came to Caesarea.
Paul's company stayed in his house at Caesarea; there the prophet Agabus foretold Paul's binding at Jerusalem.
The last verse that names him is Acts 21:8. Scripture does not record his death.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Chosen as one of the Seven.

places.name: Samaria
places.note: “The city of Samaria” where he preached (Acts 8:5).

places.name: Gaza (the desert road toward it)
places.note: He was sent to the road from Jerusalem “unto Gaza, which is desert”; the meeting place on the road is not named.

places.name: Ethiopia
places.note: Home of the official he baptized.

places.name: Azotus (Ashdod)
places.note: Where he was “found” after the baptism.

places.name: Caesarea
places.note: His home when Paul visited.

places.name: Hierapolis (in tradition)
places.note: Polycrates and Proclus (about 190-200) place a Philip and his daughters here; which Philip is disputed.

claim.text: Chosen with him as one of the Seven.
Sent with John by the apostles to Samaria after Philip's preaching there.
Sent with Peter to Samaria after Philip's preaching there.
Believed, was baptized and “continued with Philip”.
“An eunuch of great authority under Candace”, whom Philip taught from Isaiah and baptized.
Stayed many days in his house at Caesarea on the way to Jerusalem.
Came to Philip's house and foretold Paul's arrest.

scripture.text: Scripture last shows him at home in Caesarea with his four daughters (Acts 21:8-9) and records nothing of his death.

tradition.text: “Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who sleeps in Hierapolis, and his two aged virgin daughters, and another daughter who lived in the Holy Spirit and now rests at Ephesus.”
tradition.who: Polycrates of Ephesus, letter to Victor of Rome, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.31.3

tradition.text: “There were four prophetesses, the daughters of Philip, at Hierapolis in Asia. Their tomb is there and the tomb of their father.”
tradition.who: Proclus, in the Dialogue of Gaius, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.31.4

tradition.text: Papias “heard a wonderful tale from the daughters of Philip”: that “in his time” (Philip's, McGiffert explains) one rose from the dead. Eusebius calls this Philip “the apostle”.
tradition.who: Papias, as reported by Eusebius, Church History 3.39.9

tradition.text: At Caesarea the pilgrim Paula was shown “the humble abode of Philip; and the chambers of his daughters the four virgins”.
tradition.who: Jerome, Letter 108.8 (to Eustochium)

tradition.text: Another tradition makes Philip the first bishop of Tralles in Asia, with his daughters living there. Hunter (ISBE, 1915) reports it; its earliest source has not been identified here.
tradition.who: Reported by Hunter (ISBE, 1915)

questions.question: Which Philip lived and was buried at Hierapolis? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: The apostle, one of the Twelve
views.holders: Polycrates of Ephesus (about AD 190); J. B. Lightfoot (commentary on Colossians, 1875), as reported by McGiffert; C. M. Kerr (ISBE, 1915, “Philip”), for whom “The evidence seems conclusive” that the apostle's last years were spent in Phrygia

argument.text: Polycrates calls him “one of the twelve apostles”. Lightfoot held that Polycrates was right and that the apostle, not the evangelist, was buried there.

views.label: The evangelist, with his prophesying daughters
views.holders: Proclus (about 200), whose description matches Acts; A. C. McGiffert (1890)

argument.text: Acts gives the evangelist “four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy”, and Proclus speaks of “four prophetesses, the daughters of Philip” at Hierapolis. McGiffert thinks later generations would naturally fold the evangelist into the apostle of the same name.

views.label: One man: the two are the same Philip
views.holders: Eusebius (about 325), who quotes Polycrates on the apostle and Acts 21:8-9 on the evangelist side by side

argument.text: Eusebius sets the two reports together without comment, as if of one man; McGiffert notes that Eusebius took the apostle and the evangelist to be identical.

questions.question: Were the Seven the first “deacons”? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Yes: the first deacons
views.holders: Irenaeus (about AD 180), the first known to say so; Cyprian; “almost all scholars” in McGiffert's day, Lightfoot among them; Easton (1897); Souvay (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1912)

argument.text: Irenaeus calls Stephen the one “who was chosen the first deacon by the apostles”. Acts uses the related words for their “daily ministration” and to “serve tables”.

views.label: No: an office for this one task
views.holders: John Chrysostom (Homily 14 on Acts, about AD 400); in modern times Vitringa and Stanley, as reported by McGiffert

argument.text: Chrysostom asks whether theirs was the rank of deacons, and answers that “neither Deacons nor Presbyters is their designation: but it was for this particular purpose that they were ordained.”

views.label: No: the first of the Jerusalem “elders”
views.holders: Böhmer, Ritschl, Lange and Lechler, as reported by McGiffert; A. C. McGiffert (1890)

argument.text: Luke never calls the Seven deacons; the apostles' own work is called a “ministry” in the same passage; and when the elders first appear they receive the relief sent from Antioch, the kind of task the Seven were chosen for.

notSaid: Scripture does not say where Philip came from, how he came to believe, or why he is called “the evangelist”.
Scripture does not name his daughters, say what their prophesying was, or tell what became of the family after Acts 21.
Scripture does not tell how or where he died.

apostles.name: Barnabas
otherNames: Joses (KJV, Acts 4:36); Joseph in the Revised Version
apostles.title: Called an apostle with Paul (Acts 14:14)
apostles.tagline: The Levite from Cyprus who vouched for Saul, taught with him at Antioch, and went out with him on the first journey.

home.text: “A Levite, and of the country of Cyprus” (Acts 4:36); Acts first finds him in the Jerusalem church.

trade.text: Scripture gives him no trade. He “having land, sold it” for the common fund (Acts 4:37), and Paul's question “Or I only and Barnabas, have not we power to forbear working?” (1 Corinthians 9:6) speaks of the two of them working for their living.

family.text: Mark is “sister's son to Barnabas” in the KJV (Colossians 4:10). The Greek word, anepsios, is rendered “cousin” in the Revised Version (1881); Jacobs (ISBE, 1915) notes it is used in Numbers 36:11 for the sons of a father's brothers.

Our person data makes Barnabas the brother of Mary, the mother of John Mark. That rests on the KJV's “sister's son”; with “cousin” the link is less close, and Scripture does not say how they were related.

identifications.text: His name was Joses (Joseph in other Greek texts); the apostles “surnamed” him Barnabas, “which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation”.
The Revised Version (1881) renders the same words “Son of exhortation”; the Greek word, paraklēsis, carries both senses.
How the name itself means this is debated: Jacobs (ISBE, 1915) derives it from bar, “son”, and a Hebrew word for prophecy, and reports Deissmann's suggestion that it meant “son of Nebo”.
Luke calls him “a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith”, and with Paul one of “the apostles” at Lystra.

Lightfoot (1890) holds that “the apostleship of Barnabas is beyond question”, since Luke records his sending at the same time and in the same way as Paul's (Acts 13:2-3). He was not one of the Twelve.
Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200) calls him one of the Seventy (Luke 10:1) and “a fellow-worker of Paul”; McGiffert notes the tradition can be traced “no further than Clement”.
Luther and Calvin took “the brother, whose praise is in the gospel” (2 Corinthians 8:18) to be Barnabas, as Jacobs (ISBE, 1915) reports. The verse names no one.

quote.text: they sent forth Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch.

claim.text: When the church at Jerusalem heard that Greeks at Antioch had believed, it sent Barnabas; he “was glad, and exhorted them all”, and “much people was added unto the Lord”.

quote.text: Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.

claim.text: Among the prophets and teachers at Antioch, he and Saul were set apart by the Holy Ghost; the church fasted, prayed, laid hands on them and sent them away.

acts.text: He sold land he owned and laid the money at the apostles' feet.
When the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of the converted Saul, Barnabas “took him, and brought him to the apostles” and told how he had seen the Lord and preached boldly at Damascus.
At Antioch he went to Tarsus to find Saul and brought him back; for a whole year they taught there, “And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.”
He and Saul carried the Antioch church's famine relief to the elders in Judaea, and came back with John Mark.
On the first journey they preached at Salamis and crossed Cyprus to Paphos, where the deputy Sergius Paulus “called for Barnabas and Saul” and believed.
At Antioch in Pisidia “Paul and Barnabas waxed bold”: “lo, we turn to the Gentiles”; they were expelled and went on to Iconium.
At Lystra the crowd “called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius”; the two tore their clothes and stopped the sacrifice. After Paul was stoned, he left with Barnabas for Derbe.
Returning, they ordained elders in every church and told the church at Antioch how God “had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles”.

Until Paphos Acts says “Barnabas and Saul” (11:30; 12:25; 13:2, 7); from there it mostly says “Paul and Barnabas” (13:43, 46, 50; 15:2, 22, 35), though “Barnabas and Paul” comes back at Lystra and in Jerusalem (14:14; 15:12, 25).

Over circumcision, he and Paul had “no small dissension” with men from Judaea and went up to Jerusalem; at the council the multitude “gave audience to Barnabas and Paul”, and the letter called them “our beloved Barnabas and Paul, Men that have hazarded their lives”.
Paul writes that he went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, and that James, Cephas and John gave “to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship”.
At Antioch, when Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles, “Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation”.

Barnabas wanted to take John Mark on a second journey; Paul refused, because Mark had left them in Pamphylia. “The contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder”; Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus.
Acts does not mention him again after Acts 15:39. Paul still names him in 1 Corinthians 9:6, and in Colossians 4:10 tells the church to receive Mark, “sister's son to Barnabas”.

places.name: Cyprus
places.note: His home country; first stop of the first journey; where he sailed with Mark.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where he sold his land, brought Saul to the apostles, and came for the council.

places.name: Antioch (Syria)
places.note: Where he and Saul taught for a whole year, and from where they were sent out.

places.name: Tarsus
places.note: Where he went to find Saul.

places.name: Seleucia
places.note: The port they sailed from.

places.name: Salamis
places.note: First preaching on Cyprus, in the synagogues.

places.name: Paphos
places.note: Sergius Paulus believed; Elymas was struck blind.

places.name: Perga
places.note: Where John Mark left them; they preached there on the way back.

places.name: Antioch in Pisidia
places.note: “We turn to the Gentiles”; expelled from the district.

places.name: Iconium
places.note: A long stay, then flight from a plot to stone them.

places.name: Lystra
places.note: Hailed as Jupiter.

places.name: Derbe
places.note: Taught many before turning back.

places.name: Attalia
places.note: The port of the return voyage.

places.name: Salamis (his death, in tradition)
places.note: The Acts of Barnabas (written before 478) has him burned to death here.

claim.text: He vouched for Saul in Jerusalem, brought him to Antioch, and worked with him through the first journey and the council, until they parted over Mark.
His relative (Colossians 4:10); taken to Antioch and on the first journey, and later to Cyprus.
A prophet or teacher with him at Antioch.
A prophet or teacher with him at Antioch.
A prophet or teacher with him at Antioch, “brought up with Herod the tetrarch”.
Sent with Barnabas and Paul to carry the council's letter to Antioch.
Sent with them to Antioch; Paul later chose Silas when he and Barnabas parted.
Went up to Jerusalem with Paul and Barnabas.
The deputy of Cyprus who called for Barnabas and Saul and believed.
Gave him and Paul the right hand of fellowship; at Antioch Barnabas followed Peter's withdrawal from the Gentiles.

scripture.text: Scripture does not record his death. Acts last shows him sailing to Cyprus with Mark (Acts 15:39).

tradition.text: Barnabas is seized in the synagogue at Salamis at the urging of Bar-jesus, dragged out of the city with a rope round his neck, and burned; Mark hides the ashes in a cave and sails to Alexandria. The work is told in Mark's name.
tradition.who: The Journeyings and Martyrdom of St. Barnabas the Apostle (the Acts of Barnabas)
tradition.when: written before AD 478, says the introduction in the Ante-Nicene Fathers; McGiffert dates it once to the 5th century and once to the 3rd

tradition.text: In 478, it is said, the body of Barnabas was found in Cyprus.
tradition.who: Reported in the introduction to the apocryphal Acts, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 8 (1886)

tradition.text: A list of the Seventy printed among the doubtful works of Hippolytus names “Barnabas, bishop of Milan”. McGiffert calls the silence of Ambrose, bishop of Milan in the 4th century, “a sufficient proof of its groundlessness”.
tradition.who: “On the Seventy Apostles”, attributed to Hippolytus
tradition.when: date unknown; its editor calls it “Probably spurious, but yet antique”

writings.title: Hebrews: Tertullian named Barnabas as its writer; the letter names none (see the question below and the Hebrews page)

questions.question: Did Barnabas write the letter to the Hebrews? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Yes
views.holders: Tertullian, On Modesty 20 (not earlier than AD 208); in modern times Grau and Zahn, as reported by Jacobs (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: Tertullian quotes Hebrews 6 from “an Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of Barnabas”, calling him “a man sufficiently accredited by God”.

views.label: Not settled: one of several names
views.holders: Jerome (392), who gives Barnabas “according to Tertullian” beside Luke and Clement; Fenlon (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1907), who thinks Tertullian's credit “probably” false

argument.text: Jerome reports that the letter is not counted Paul's “on account of its difference from the others in style and language”, and lists the other names offered. The full views are on the Hebrews page.

questions.question: Did Barnabas write the “Epistle of Barnabas”, a letter outside the New Testament? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Yes
views.holders: Clement of Alexandria (about 200), who quotes it as “the Apostle Barnabas”; Jerome (392), who still placed it “among the apocryphal writings”; Archbishop Wake and Lardner, as reported by Coxe (1885)

argument.text: McGiffert notes that the ancient testimony names Barnabas the companion of Paul “without a dissenting voice”, though Eusebius (about 325) listed “the extant epistle of Barnabas” among the rejected writings.

views.label: No: a later writer
views.holders: A. C. Coxe (1885), who places its writer in the times of Trajan and Hadrian; A. C. McGiffert (1890); J. B. Lightfoot, as quoted by Jacobs (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: The letter names no writer. McGiffert finds its contents “conclusive against ‘the Levite Barnabas’ as the author”; Lightfoot suggests “some unknown namesake”.

questions.question: When did Barnabas die? (Scripture does not say; the proposals are listed by date.)

views.label: In the 50s: AD 53 or 56
views.holders: Ceillier and Papebroch (53); Braunsberger (56), as listed by E. C. Richardson in his notes to Jerome (1892)

argument.text: Richardson adds that the question of the date “is a good deal mixed up with the question of the authenticity” of the Epistle of Barnabas.

views.label: Alive when Paul wrote 1 Corinthians, probably dead before Colossians
views.holders: J. F. Fenlon (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1907)

argument.text: Paul names him as still at work in 1 Corinthians 9:6, which Fenlon dates 56 or 57; that Mark was later with Paul during his imprisonment (Colossians 4:10) “is regarded as an indication that Barnabas was no longer living”, which Fenlon thinks probable.

views.label: Later: AD 61 or 76
views.holders: the Roman Breviary (61); Nirschl (76), as listed by Richardson (1892)

argument.text: Richardson's note gives both dates without their reasons.

notSaid: Scripture does not say when or how Barnabas came to believe, or where the land he sold lay.
Scripture does not say whether he and Paul were reconciled after Acts 15, though Paul names him without blame in 1 Corinthians 9:6.
Scripture does not tell how or when he died.

apostles.name: John Mark
apostles.title: “John, whose surname was Mark” (Acts 12:12)
apostles.tagline: Son of a Jerusalem household where the church prayed; left the first journey, and was later “profitable” to Paul.

home.text: His mother Mary had a house in Jerusalem where “many were gathered together praying” the night Peter was freed from prison.

family.text: His mother was Mary, at whose house the believers met.
Paul calls him “sister's son to Barnabas” in the KJV; the Greek word is rendered “cousin” in the Revised Version (1881).

Peter calls him “Marcus my son” (1 Peter 5:13). Smith (1884) takes it that Mark “probably owed his conversion” to Peter; MacRory (1910) that the word “need not be taken to imply more than affectionate regard for a younger man”.

identifications.text: Acts calls him “John, whose surname was Mark” (12:12, 25; 15:37), then just “John” (13:5, 13), then “Mark” (15:39); Paul and Peter write “Marcus” or “Mark” (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11; 1 Peter 5:13). Our person data holds all of these as one man; whether they are is a question below.
Papias, early in the 2nd century, passes on from “the presbyter” that Mark became “the interpreter of Peter”. The Gospel that bears his name does not name its writer.

Hippolytus, early in the 3rd century, calls him “Mark, he of the maimed finger”. MacRory (1910) lists the explanations later offered: that he cut off his thumb to unfit himself for the priesthood, that his fingers were naturally short, or that the word is a figure for “deserted”.

The preface to his Gospel in manuscripts of the Latin Vulgate calls him a Levite who had served as a priest in Israel. MacRory notes that early writers are silent and that it may be “only an inference from his relation to Barnabas the Levite”. Our person data also gives him the tribe of Levi.

quote.text: took with them John, whose surname was Mark.

claim.text: Barnabas and Saul, returning from the famine relief at Jerusalem, brought him back with them to Antioch.

quote.text: and they had also John to their minister.

claim.text: At Salamis on Cyprus he served Barnabas and Saul. MacRory (1910) notes that “the vagueness and variety of meaning of the Greek term” translated “minister” leaves his task uncertain.

acts.text: Peter, freed from prison by the angel, went to the house of “Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark”.
He went with Barnabas and Saul through Cyprus, but at Perga in Pamphylia “John departing from them returned to Jerusalem”.
When Barnabas wanted to take him on the second journey, Paul refused, since he “departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work”; Barnabas took him and sailed to Cyprus.

Later he is with Paul while Paul is “in bonds”, and Paul tells the Colossians to receive him if he comes; he is one of the few “of the circumcision” who are Paul's “fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God” and “a comfort” to him.
Paul names him among “my fellowlabourers” in the letter to Philemon.
In 2 Timothy Paul writes: “Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.”
Peter sends greetings from “The church that is at Babylon … and so doth Marcus my son”.
Colossians and Philemon do not say where Paul was imprisoned, and which city 1 Peter 5:13 means by “Babylon” is disputed (see the Letters page for 1 Peter).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: His mother's house; where he went back from Perga.

places.name: Antioch (Syria)
places.note: Brought here by Barnabas and Saul; where Paul and Barnabas parted over him.

places.name: Salamis
places.note: Serving Barnabas and Saul on Cyprus.

places.name: Paphos
places.note: The party sailed from here to Perga.

places.name: Perga
places.note: Where he left them.

places.name: Cyprus
places.note: Sailed there with Barnabas.

places.name: Colossae
places.note: Paul expected he might come to the church there.

places.name: Babylon (1 Peter 5:13)
places.note: Where Mark was with Peter; whether this is Rome by a figure or another city is disputed, so no pin is drawn.

places.name: Rome (in tradition)
places.note: Clement of Alexandria (about 200): Mark wrote down Peter's preaching at Rome.

places.name: Alexandria (in tradition)
places.note: Eusebius (about 325), “they say”: Mark founded the church there; Jerome (392): buried there.

claim.text: Her house in Jerusalem was a meeting place of the church.
His relative; took him to Antioch, on the first journey and to Cyprus.
Took him on the first journey, refused him for the second, and later called him a fellow-worker and “profitable to me for the ministry”.
Came to his mother's house after his escape; sends greetings from “Marcus my son”.
With him and Paul in the greetings of Colossians and Philemon.
Named with him as one of Paul's Jewish fellow-workers.
Named with him among Paul's fellow-labourers; “Only Luke is with me”, Paul writes when he asks for Mark.
Named with him among Paul's fellow-labourers.
Asked to bring Mark with him to Paul.

person.name: Silvanus
person.note: Our person data takes him to be the Silas of Acts; 1 Peter does not say so.

claim.text: Named with him at the close of 1 Peter.

scripture.text: Scripture does not record Mark's death. His last mentions are 2 Timothy 4:11 and 1 Peter 5:13; which of the two is later is not known.

tradition.text: “And they say that this Mark was the first that was sent to Egypt, and that he proclaimed the Gospel which he had written, and first established churches in Alexandria.”
tradition.who: Eusebius, Church History 2.16.1

tradition.text: “When Nero was in the eighth year of his reign, Annianus succeeded Mark the evangelist in the administration of the parish of Alexandria.”
tradition.who: Eusebius, Church History 2.24
tradition.when: about AD 325; Nero's eighth year is AD 62 (McGiffert)

tradition.text: “He died in the eighth year of Nero and was buried at Alexandria, Annianus succeeding him.” MacRory (1910) thinks this is probably drawn from Eusebius, and notes that if Mark was alive when 2 Timothy was written he cannot have died in 61-62.
tradition.who: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 8

tradition.text: The Acts of Mark give him a martyr's death, dragged through the streets of Alexandria. MacRory: “we have no evidence earlier than the fourth century that the saint was martyred”, though he adds that this silence “is not at all decisive against the truth of the later traditions”.
tradition.who: The Acts of Mark, as reported by MacRory (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910)

tradition.text: Venetians later carried his remains from Alexandria to Venice; Farmer (ISBE, 1915) gives the year as 815.
tradition.who: Venetian tradition, as reported by Farmer (ISBE, 1915)

writings.title: The Gospel according to Mark (its traditional title)

questions.question: Is John Mark of Acts the same man as the Mark of Paul's letters, of 1 Peter, and of the Gospel? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: One man
views.holders: Eusebius (about 325) and Jerome (392), who join the Gospel's Mark to Peter's “Marcus my son”; A. C. McGiffert (1890); Smith (1884); Easton (1897); MacRory (1910), who says the identity “is not questioned by any ancient writer of note”

argument.text: The Mark of Colossians is Barnabas's relative, and Acts ties John Mark closely to Barnabas; the Mark Peter calls his son fits the son of Mary, at whose house Peter took refuge.

views.label: Several men
views.holders: The list “On the Seventy Apostles” among the doubtful works of Hippolytus (date unknown, “Probably spurious, but yet antique”); the Greek church's calendar, which MacRory notes keeps a feast of Mark the evangelist on 25 April and of John Mark on 27 September

argument.text: That list names three: “Mark the evangelist, bishop of Alexandria”, “Mark, cousin to Barnabas, bishop of Apollonia”, and “Mark, who is also John, bishop of Bibloupolis”.

questions.question: What do the early writers say about Mark, Peter and the Gospel? (In date order; they do not agree on the details.)

views.label: Mark wrote down what Peter taught, “though not indeed in order”
views.holders: “The presbyter”, as quoted by Papias (early 2nd century), in Eusebius 3.39.15

argument.text: Mark “wrote down accurately, though not indeed in order, whatsoever he remembered of the things said or done by Christ.” “For he neither heard the Lord nor followed him, but afterward … he followed Peter”.

views.label: After Peter's and Paul's death
views.holders: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1 (about 180)

argument.text: “After their departure Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, also transmitted to us in writing those things which Peter had preached.”

views.label: At Rome in Peter's lifetime; Peter “neither directly forbade nor encouraged it”
views.holders: Clement of Alexandria, Hypotyposes (about 200), in Eusebius 6.14.6-7

argument.text: Hearers of Peter's preaching at Rome asked Mark, “who had followed him for a long time and remembered his sayings”, to write them out.

views.label: In Peter's lifetime, and with Peter's approval
views.holders: Origen (about 245 or later), in Eusebius 6.25.5; Eusebius himself (2.15, about 325); Jerome (392)

argument.text: Origen: Mark “composed it according to the instructions of Peter”. Eusebius says Peter “was pleased” and gave the work “the sanction of his authority”, citing Clement; McGiffert notes that this “contradicts the account of Clement”.

questions.question: Was Mark the young man who fled naked when Jesus was arrested (Mark 14:51-52)? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: Probably he was
views.holders: Easton (1897: “It is probable”); “many”, as MacRory (1910) reports

argument.text: Only Mark's Gospel tells the incident, and it names no one.

views.label: There is no sign of it; Mark had not followed Jesus
views.holders: “The presbyter” quoted by Papias (early 2nd century): Mark “neither heard the Lord nor followed him”

argument.text: MacRory notes that this statement “need not be pressed too strictly, nor force us to believe that he never saw Christ”.

questions.question: Why did John Mark turn back at Perga? (Scripture does not say; views in the order they were published.)

views.label: He did not like the work, or wanted to see his mother
views.holders: Matthew Henry (1706-1721)

argument.text: Henry offers both reasons as guesses and adds that Mark left “without the consent of Paul and Barnabas”.

views.label: No reason can be known
views.holders: Smith (1884: “for some unexplained reason”); Fenlon (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1907: Luke “does not state”)

argument.text: Acts gives only Paul's later complaint that Mark “went not with them to the work”.

views.label: He shrank from the toil
views.holders: MacRory (1910), who says Acts 15:38 “seems to suggest that he feared the toil”

argument.text: The journey after Perga led inland to Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium and Lystra.

views.label: He objected to offering salvation to Gentiles on faith alone
views.holders: J. H. Farmer (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: Farmer points to the conversion of Sergius Paulus at Paphos just before, where Paul takes the lead, and to Paul's strong words in Acts 15:38.

notSaid: Scripture never names Mark's father, says how he came to believe, or says why he left at Perga.
The Gospel of Mark does not name its writer; the link to this Mark comes from Papias and later writers.
Scripture does not say where Paul was imprisoned when he wrote of Mark in Colossians and Philemon, or record how or where Mark died.
